title: What are the core concepts of AWS CloudFormation — templates (YAML/JSON) with Resources/Parameters/Mappings/Outputs/Conditions, Stacks, Change Sets (preview changes before applying), Drift Detection, nested stacks and StackSets (multi-account/multi-region) — and how does SAM relate to it (a CloudFormation transform/macro for serverless)?
shortTitle: AWS CloudFormation — core concepts and how SAM relates
topicTitle: What are the core concepts of AWS CloudFormation

s1_definition.profdef: AWS CloudFormation is AWS's native Infrastructure as Code service. You write a template in YAML or JSON that declares resources and their configuration, and CloudFormation provisions them as a single managed unit called a Stack. Templates have well-defined sections: Resources, Parameters, Mappings, Outputs, and Conditions. Change Sets preview what an update will do before you apply it, Drift Detection reports manual changes, nested stacks and StackSets enable composition and multi-account/multi-region rollout, and SAM is a CloudFormation transform that adds concise shorthand for serverless resources.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a CloudFormation template as the official construction blueprint for a National Bank of India branch, and the Stack as the finished branch built from that blueprint and tracked as one unit. Parameters are the blanks you fill in per branch — city, size, vault capacity. Mappings are a lookup chart, like "in Mumbai use this ATM model, in Delhi use that one." Conditions are the rules, like "only build a drive-through if this is a highway branch." Outputs are the key facts posted at the end, like the branch's phone number. A Change Set is the architect showing you a marked-up drawing of exactly what will change before any wall is touched, and Drift Detection is an inspector checking whether anyone moved a wall without updating the blueprint.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** AWS CloudFormation is AWS's native Infrastructure as Code service. You write a template in YAML or JSON that declares resources and their configuration, and CloudFormation provisions them as a single managed unit called a Stack. Templates have well-defined sections: Resources, Parameters, Mappings, Outputs, and Conditions. Change Sets preview what an update will do before you apply it, Drift Detection reports manual changes, nested stacks and StackSets enable composition and multi-account/multi-region rollout, and SAM is a CloudFormation transform that adds concise shorthand for serverless resources.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a CloudFormation template as the official construction blueprint for a National Bank of India branch, and the Stack as the finished branch built from that blueprint and tracked as one unit. Parameters are the blanks you fill in per branch — city, size, vault capacity. Mappings are a lookup chart, like "in Mumbai use this ATM model, in Delhi use that one." Conditions are the rules, like "only build a drive-through if this is a highway branch." Outputs are the key facts posted at the end, like the branch's phone number. A Change Set is the architect showing you a marked-up drawing of exactly what will change before any wall is touched, and Drift Detection is an inspector checking whether anyone moved a wall without updating the blueprint.

**One line to remember:** CloudFormation turns a YAML/JSON template into a managed Stack, with Change Sets to preview, Drift Detection to catch manual edits, StackSets for multi-account rollout, and SAM as serverless shorthand.

sections.s2_technical:
A template is the document you write. Its most important section is Resources, where you declare each AWS resource with a logical name, a type like `AWS::S3::Bucket`, and its properties. This is the only required section. Parameters let callers pass values in at deploy time, like an environment name or an instance size, so one template serves many situations. You reference a parameter with the `!Ref` intrinsic function, for example `BucketName: !Ref Environment`.

Mappings are static lookup tables inside the template. A classic use is picking a value by region or environment — you define a map of region to AMI id, then look it up with `!FindInMap`. Conditions let you include or configure resources only when a test passes; you define a condition like `IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Environment, production]` and then attach it to a resource or use it in an `!If`. Outputs publish values after the Stack is created — a database endpoint, a queue URL — and other stacks can import these across stack boundaries.

A Stack is the running instance of a template. Everything CloudFormation creates from one template is grouped into that Stack, and the Stack is the unit you create, update, and delete. Deleting the Stack deletes all its resources (unless you mark some to retain). CloudFormation tracks the state of the Stack for you on the server side, so there is no state file to store. If a create or update fails partway, CloudFormation automatically rolls the Stack back to its last good state, which is a strong safety property.

A Change Set is CloudFormation's preview mechanism. Before applying an update, you create a Change Set from the new template, and CloudFormation shows exactly which resources will be added, modified, or removed, and critically whether a change requires replacement — destroying and recreating a resource. For a bank this is essential: you never want to discover that renaming a database caused it to be deleted and recreated. You review the Change Set, then execute it.

Drift Detection answers "has anyone changed this Stack by hand outside CloudFormation." You trigger drift detection on a Stack and CloudFormation compares the real resources against the template's expected configuration, reporting any resource that has drifted and exactly which properties differ. This catches the dangerous situation where someone edits a resource in the console and the template no longer reflects reality.

Nested stacks let you break a big template into smaller reusable child templates — a networking child, a database child — referenced from a parent via `AWS::CloudFormation::Stack`. This keeps templates manageable and promotes reuse. StackSets go further: they let you deploy the same Stack across many AWS accounts and many regions from one place, which is exactly how a large bank rolls out a standard security baseline to every account and region consistently.

SAM, the Serverless Application Model, is not a separate tool fighting CloudFormation; it is built on top of it. A SAM template is a CloudFormation template with the line `Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31` at the top, which tells CloudFormation to run the SAM macro. That macro expands concise serverless resource types — `AWS::Serverless::Function`, `AWS::Serverless::Api`, `AWS::Serverless::SimpleTable` — into the much larger set of plain CloudFormation resources they imply. So writing one `AWS::Serverless::Function` with an event source automatically generates the Lambda function, its IAM role, and the API Gateway wiring. Under the hood it is still CloudFormation, still a Stack, still Change Sets and rollback. A senior-level nuance: because a Transform is just a macro, you can mix SAM serverless resources and ordinary CloudFormation resources in the same template, which is common when a serverless function needs a regular SQS queue or DynamoDB table alongside it.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India is building a serverless fraud-alert feature. When a suspicious transaction is detected, a Lambda function processes it and writes an alert record to DynamoDB, exposed through an API Gateway endpoint. The platform team must also roll out a standard logging bucket to every AWS account the bank owns.

Problem 1 — the team keeps copy-pasting the same forty lines of CloudFormation just to create one Lambda plus its IAM role plus its API Gateway route. This is exactly what SAM solves — one concise `AWS::Serverless::Function` block with an `Api` event expands into all of that automatically via the SAM transform.

Problem 2 — during a past update, renaming a resource silently caused it to be replaced, briefly dropping the fraud endpoint. This is exactly what Change Sets prevent — the preview clearly flags "requires replacement" before anything happens.

Problem 3 — someone once edited the fraud Lambda's memory setting in the console, and nobody knew the template was now out of date. This is exactly what Drift Detection catches — it reports the drifted property.

Problem 4 — the compliance team needs an identical logging bucket in all fifteen AWS accounts across two regions. This is exactly what StackSets do — deploy one Stack definition everywhere from a single place.

The mini-project shows a SAM template for the fraud-alert function with Parameters, Conditions, and Outputs, a plain nested-stack reference, the StackSets idea for the logging baseline, and the Change Set and drift commands. A Java snippet shows the Lambda handler that processes a suspicious transaction.

sections.s4d_java:
```yaml
# File: template.yaml
# The Transform line turns this into a SAM template: CloudFormation runs
# the SAM macro to expand the concise serverless types below.
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Transform: AWS::Serverless-2016-10-31        # <-- this is what makes it SAM
Description: Fraud-alert serverless stack for National Bank of India

Parameters:                                   # caller-supplied values
  Environment:
    Type: String
    AllowedValues: [staging, production]

Mappings:                                     # static lookup table
  MemoryByEnv:
    staging:    { MB: 256 }
    production: { MB: 1024 }

Conditions:                                   # include things only in prod
  IsProd: !Equals [!Ref Environment, production]

Resources:
  # ONE concise serverless function. The SAM macro expands this into a
  # Lambda function + IAM role + API Gateway route behind the scenes.
  FraudAlertFunction:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::Function
    Properties:
      FunctionName: !Sub "nbi-fraud-alert-${Environment}"
      Runtime: java21
      Handler: com.bank.fraud.FraudAlertHandler::handleRequest
      MemorySize: !FindInMap [MemoryByEnv, !Ref Environment, MB]
      CodeUri: target/fraud-alert-1.0.0.jar
      Events:
        Api:                                  # auto-creates API Gateway wiring
          Type: Api
          Properties:
            Path: /alerts
            Method: post
      Policies:
        - DynamoDBCrudPolicy: { TableName: !Ref AlertTable }

  # A plain SAM/CloudFormation DynamoDB table (mix serverless + normal).
  AlertTable:
    Type: AWS::Serverless::SimpleTable
    Properties:
      TableName: !Sub "nbi-fraud-alerts-${Environment}"

  # Enable point-in-time recovery ONLY in production, via a Condition.
  ProdBackupAlarm:
    Type: AWS::CloudWatch::Alarm
    Condition: IsProd
    Properties:
      AlarmName: !Sub "nbi-fraud-errors-${Environment}"
      MetricName: Errors
      Namespace: AWS/Lambda
      ComparisonOperator: GreaterThanThreshold
      Threshold: 0
      EvaluationPeriods: 1
      Period: 60
      Statistic: Sum

Outputs:                                       # published after create
  AlertApiUrl:
    Description: POST endpoint for fraud alerts
    Value: !Sub "https://${ServerlessRestApi}.execute-api.${AWS::Region}.amazonaws.com/Prod/alerts"
  AlertTableName:
    Value: !Ref AlertTable
```

```yaml
# File: nested/logging-bucket.yaml
# A reusable CHILD template. Referenced by a parent via AWS::CloudFormation::Stack,
# and deployed to EVERY account/region using a StackSet (see run instructions).
AWSTemplateFormatVersion: "2010-09-09"
Parameters:
  AccountLabel: { Type: String }
Resources:
  LoggingBucket:
    Type: AWS::S3::Bucket
    Properties:
      BucketName: !Sub "nbi-central-logs-${AccountLabel}"
      BucketEncryption:
        ServerSideEncryptionConfiguration:
          - ServerSideEncryptionByDefault: { SSEAlgorithm: aws:kms }
      PublicAccessBlockConfiguration:
        BlockPublicAcls: true
        BlockPublicPolicy: true
        IgnorePublicAcls: true
        RestrictPublicBuckets: true
```

```java
// ─── File: src/main/java/com/bank/fraud/FraudAlertHandler.java ───
package com.bank.fraud;

import com.amazonaws.services.lambda.runtime.Context;
import com.amazonaws.services.lambda.runtime.RequestHandler;
import java.math.BigDecimal;
import java.util.Map;

// The Lambda that the ONE AWS::Serverless::Function block deploys.
// Processes a suspicious transaction and records an alert.
public class FraudAlertHandler implements RequestHandler<Map<String, String>, String> {

    @Override
    public String handleRequest(Map<String, String> event, Context ctx) {
        String accountId = event.get("accountId");               // e.g. SAV2001
        BigDecimal amount = new BigDecimal(event.get("amount"));  // money -> BigDecimal

        // A simple rule: flag transfers above 500,000 rupees for review.
        BigDecimal threshold = new BigDecimal("500000");
        boolean suspicious = amount.compareTo(threshold) > 0;

        if (suspicious) {
            ctx.getLogger().log("FRAUD ALERT account=" + accountId + " amount=" + amount);
            // In real code: write an alert row to the DynamoDB AlertTable here.
            return "{\"status\":\"ALERT_RAISED\",\"account\":\"" + accountId + "\"}";
        }
        return "{\"status\":\"CLEARED\",\"account\":\"" + accountId + "\"}";
    }
}
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the Lambda jar first.
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# SAM build + guided deploy. 'sam deploy' creates a Stack via CloudFormation.
sam build
sam deploy --guided \
  --stack-name nbi-fraud-alert-prod \
  --parameter-overrides Environment=production

# Preview an UPDATE with a Change Set before applying (no changes yet):
aws cloudformation create-change-set \
  --stack-name nbi-fraud-alert-prod \
  --change-set-name bump-memory \
  --template-body file://template.yaml \
  --parameters ParameterKey=Environment,ParameterValue=production \
  --capabilities CAPABILITY_IAM
aws cloudformation describe-change-set --change-set-name bump-memory \
  --stack-name nbi-fraud-alert-prod   # shows Add/Modify/Remove + Replacement

# Catch manual console edits with Drift Detection:
aws cloudformation detect-stack-drift --stack-name nbi-fraud-alert-prod

# Roll out the logging bucket to EVERY account + region via a StackSet:
aws cloudformation create-stack-set \
  --stack-set-name nbi-central-logging \
  --template-body file://nested/logging-bucket.yaml
aws cloudformation create-stack-instances \
  --stack-set-name nbi-central-logging \
  --accounts 111111111111 222222222222 \
  --regions ap-south-1 us-east-1
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: the team deploys the fraud-alert stack to production, then later bumps the Lambda memory, and finally checks for drift.

Step 1: On the first deploy, CloudFormation reads template.yaml, sees the Transform line, and runs the SAM macro. The macro expands the single `AWS::Serverless::Function` into a full Lambda function, an IAM execution role, and API Gateway resources. CloudFormation groups all of them into the Stack `nbi-fraud-alert-prod`.

Step 2: CloudFormation resolves `!FindInMap [MemoryByEnv, production, MB]` to 1024, so the Lambda is created with 1 GB of memory. Because the Environment is production, the `IsProd` condition is true, so the CloudWatch error alarm is also created. In staging it would be skipped.

Step 3: The Stack finishes and publishes Outputs — the alert API URL and the table name. The team reads the API URL to wire up the mobile app.

Step 4: Later the team edits the memory mapping and creates a Change Set. CloudFormation computes that the Lambda will be Modified, not Replaced, and shows this in the Change Set. The team confirms it is a safe in-place update and executes it.

Step 5: Someone edits the Lambda's timeout in the console by hand. The team runs detect-stack-drift. CloudFormation compares the live resource against the template and reports the Lambda as DRIFTED with the timeout property differing, prompting the team to fix the template.

Step 6: Separately, the StackSet pushes the logging bucket into two accounts and two regions, creating four identical encrypted buckets from one definition.

sections.s6_takeaway:
CloudFormation is AWS's native Infrastructure as Code service. You write a template in YAML or JSON, and the heart of it is the Resources section where you declare each AWS resource. Parameters let callers pass in values at deploy time so one template serves many situations, Mappings are static lookup tables you query with FindInMap, Conditions include or configure resources only when a test passes, and Outputs publish values like an endpoint after the stack is built. CloudFormation provisions everything from one template as a single managed unit called a Stack, and it tracks the Stack's state for you on the server side, so there is no state file to store.

Three operational concepts matter a lot in a bank. Change Sets are the preview — before applying an update, CloudFormation shows exactly which resources will be added, modified, or removed, and crucially whether a change forces a replacement, so you never accidentally destroy a database by renaming it. Drift Detection answers whether anyone changed the Stack by hand outside CloudFormation, comparing the live resources against the template and reporting the exact drifted properties. And if a create or update fails partway, CloudFormation automatically rolls the whole Stack back to its last good state.

For scale and reuse, nested stacks let you split a big template into reusable child templates referenced from a parent, and StackSets let you deploy the same Stack across many AWS accounts and many regions from one place — which is exactly how a large bank rolls out a standard logging or security baseline to every account consistently.

SAM, the Serverless Application Model, is not a competitor to CloudFormation; it is built on top of it. A SAM template is just a CloudFormation template with a Transform line that tells CloudFormation to run the SAM macro, which expands concise serverless types like Serverless Function into the full set of plain resources they imply — the Lambda, its IAM role, and the API Gateway wiring. Under the hood it is still a Stack with Change Sets and rollback, and you can freely mix SAM serverless resources with ordinary CloudFormation resources in the same template. On the fraud-alert feature at National Bank of India, this let us write one concise function block instead of forty lines, preview every change with a Change Set, catch a console edit with drift detection, and roll a logging bucket out to every account with a StackSet.
